blocks.x: For those who may listen to this tape, my name is John Steiner. I want to introduce Edwin Ashcraft, Squirrel Ashcraft, who's been a leader in Chicago of the Chicago-style jazz bands, both amateur and professional. And his name will be familiar to anyone in our generation who has been acquainted with the Chicago Fellows. Squirrel has played and recorded with people like Freeman and McPartland. He knew Teschmacher and knew well that Davy Tuff and Krupa has played on many occasions with the Condon gang and is currently active, as he has been for the last 30 or 40 years. I thought from a squirrel's position that he might talk with an objectivity and an unconcern about the sources of inspiration for the Chicago Fellows. And that would catch a great deal of the New Orleans influence in its first stage on its arrival to Chicago and what it did to Chicago. He then was able to observe what it did to New York. He tells me that in about 1925, when he was at school in the East, he began to visit New York and see what the popular music picture was there. He was particularly interested in the jazz aspects, and that took him close to New Orleans influences. Squirrel, would you tell us a little bit about where you were born and when and your parents and brother and sister and that sort of thing, just so that we have you identified?

Well, I was born in 1905, which was approximately when most of the Austin High School band were born. I might add that I was probably born in just about the right place at about the right time for some unusual chances to observe, and I wish I'd observed a little better. Or at least I wish I'd recorded it a little better. I'm a third-generation lawyer. My family came here from Virginia and from Massachusetts and came up from Vandalia, Illinois. I have two sisters. I've been a lawyer ever since, a member of a Chicago law firm. My first connection with jazz music was approximately the same as that of the Austin boys. I think that our, I can speak for all of them in saying that the first contact we had was through records. The, we had very little access toward anything except the original Dixieland jazz band as a jazz source, that is of a, of a, anything like a Dixieland band. And as I recall, I was depending heavily on, I was a pianist. And I think the first piano that impressed me at all was the all-star trio, Oman and Arden, later on Zez Confrey. And I was inclined to throw them all out the window the first time I had that record of Carolina Shout of James P. Johnson, which must have been in the neighborhood of the, of World War I. It was an okay record, Keep Off the Grass. It was the other side. I still have it. As far as bands were concerned, we heard lots of them, like the Happy Six, Paul Specht. But I think that the first impression that upset, this would go from a Partland, probably Freeman, certainly me. I think the first record we all heard that really made a profound impression on us was Farewell Blues by the Friars Inn band. And, this was very close to the coming of, of Bix. And Bix being a couple years older than we, which made a great deal of difference at that age, that teenage, most of us didn't really know him very well. I'm talking now about 1920, 21. I think my date would be just about right on that.
Maybe a little later, before he arrived in Chicago.
Well, I think he was in Lake Forest in 21.
Yes.

And also, it's hard for people to realize that Bix, Bix's influence on Chicago was almost entirely through records, because he generally played in Indiana. He very rarely played around Chicago. Cy Welge was his great friend at Lake Forest and a drummer. And they played together a little bit, jobbing dates.
Before he had developed a style or maybe a... Yes. Before he had heard many things.
Yeah.
Except the record you talked about.
Well, the Farewell Blues record, I remember particularly just because it was the first.
Had you known the New Orleans Rhythm Kings before you heard this record? No. You've never been to hear them?
No. I'd heard about them, but I hadn't heard them at all.
That, of course, was a Jeanette, and it was the first of a series that they made.

I believe, as late as four or five years later, that even members of the Wolverines, if pressed, would have said that they were not influenced by New Orleans music particularly. I think they were wrong, and I think most of them would probably say so today, but their impression at that point was that they were not. All, I think, would say that the original Dixieland was an awful important move in music and that they'd certainly paid attention to it, but I don't think that they felt that they were playing it.
They thought they had either developed to a new level or their sources had been too diffuse to pin it down.
I think their sources, strangely enough, were closer to Hillbilly than anything else.
Oh, so? It was a southern Indiana type of a combination of ragtime and tricky, funny music.

Now, if you realize that the Friars Inn band itself was a combination fundamentally, and don't pin me down too accurately on this, but I think it was an eight-piece band. It was fundamentally two four-piece bands. It was Mayers, of course, and George Brunas, and later on Leon Rapolo from New Orleans, white musicians from New Orleans, and Steve Brown, the bass. But fundamentally, or Deacon Loycano, rather, from New Orleans was the original bass player. But fundamentally, if you realize that the Snyder Brothers from Lower Illinois, of which Frank was the singer.
Snyder and Pettis.
Well, the two Snyders. Oh, there were two. Yeah, Frank and Ralph.
Oh, yes.
Ralph later drummed with the Wolverines. And Frank was the first drummer with that band. And Jack Pettis, you see. And then, I'm missing one. I think the original.
Well, a Chicago piano player. Well, yes. Or Schoble.

Yeah, Schoble and Carl. Forgotten I know him pretty well. We were both pallbearers at Paul's funeral. But fundamentally, the Chicagoans, two from Lower Indiana, two from Lower Illinois, farm boys, were playing as a unit in Chicago before the other people were playing.

Frank Snyder tells me about their meeting, Brunus, over here on North Avenue in Halsted, where they'd come to Jim, finding some people that they could work with. And he said that's where he met Brunus long before they joined together to form the New Orleans Rhythm Kings.
I think Pettis told me that they played as two separate, that the two four-piece bands got together as an eight-piece band, often on Sundays.
Oh, so. Before they combined.
And I think one or the other had been playing at the Erie Cafe.
Yes, Snyder. And Brunus and Merez had been playing with Rag Baby Stevens. Do you happen to know a drummer?
Yeah, I remember his name very well.

Down here on Madison Street, just about south of us, Madison and Halsted, or Madison and Ashland, in that neighborhood. Maybe Tommy Thomas' or some of the joints that were then popular in that area. That was a hot area.

Yeah. That's why I don't, I think that it wasn't until after Bud, Tesh, and the others had heard Louie, or rather heard the Oliver Band, out in the south side, that they really connected the two up. And I'm not too sure they did. They were inclined to separate the white and Negro musicians, partly because the economics of Chicago at that point had the Negro musician either playing on the south side or playing as an entertaining type of band. They used to think of moments as a clown band. And it would be only the rare few of us who were interested in music who realized that Jimmy Nunes wasn't just a funny guy, you see, and that Baby Dodds wasn't being tricky. Because he was consciously entertaining when he went out and played parties. And they had the two separate unions.
There seems to be the possibility of some direct imitation. Would you think that Tesh might have imitated, might have studied records of Johnny Dodds?

Well, Rod Kless told me that he consciously imitated Johnny Dodds, and that he was a great influence on him, which was hard for me to understand. My heroes were Larry Shields and Rapolo. But they weren't Tesh, I'm quite sure. They certainly weren't Rods. And of course, Goodman would be the only exception to my age group, because Goodman was quite a bit younger. And you can find records of Goodman's, or rather, test records, some of which have been repeated, with the Pollock Band, Unreleased Masters, where Benny sounds an awful lot like Tesh. And I'm sure he admired him like the Dickens.

That influence kept bobbing up, even into the 30s, and thinned out soon after when it became more respectable for pure tone. But I've wondered whether Tesh, finding the raspy and the hard tone so full of emotion, might have related to Bechet or to Dodds, who were so capable in using the expressive distortion of tone. And to say that it probably was a sequence isn't quite as accurate as knowing that it was. And so this question will continue to bob up.
The one who probably can answer it, of course, is Pee Wee. And Pee Wee probably could give you a very clear-cut answer on that.
Did Bud Freeman relate at all to the colored influences?
Would it be worthwhile for me to tell you about Pettis and the origin of the tenor?
Yes, sure.
Because I'd explain a little bit of this. Yes. Pettis was working for the Hoover Food Administration in the...
First floor.

Yeah, as an office boy. In the corner of Adams and LaSalle, the old building's still up there. On armistice night, or rather on fake armistice night, if you remember, that came a week early, he and the other office boy got good and plastered. And they bought, each of them bought from Land and Healy's a C. Melody Saxe vault, which were then in Vogue and all over the windows of Land and Healy. And the other office boy thought better of it the next day and took his back, and Pettis didn't. Well, after the war was over, there was nothing whatsoever to do in this office of theirs. And Jack learned to play it actually in the safe, in the vault. And he kept it, was good at it, and kept up playing. He later ran into Mel, to Schoble, who'd written Nobody's Sweetheart or a tune remarkably like it. One of the big pop tunes at the time. And he had been playing with the Friars Inn Band, in the Friars Inn, or the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, for some time before the idea of a tenor ever crossed his mind. And the only reason it ever did was because his C was busted.
You mean Pettis? Pettis. I'm sorry. Oh, I didn't remember whether you meant Schoble or not.

No, I meant Pettis. Well, he took it in to have it gone over, new springs and pads and things. And the only thing they had to lend him in the interim was a tenor. And, which was not hard for him, being a B-flat instrument. And all our tunes were B-flat, E-flat, A-flat. The only other tenors in town that I knew of, and I'm sure that he knew about, were Paul Besey, who was playing in the movie theaters, and Dyson Jones. And the only reason Jones was of any interest to anybody was because of the people in the band. You see, he had Frankie Cortell and Alf Eldridge and some very good guys in the band. The band really wasn't quite bad. It wasn't bad. Although, Eysham Jones wasn't any good, except as a writer. And Pettis loved the tenor and kept it. And he used the C and the tenor for just a short time after that and then gave up the C. ! But when they first made their, when they made their first record of Farewell Blues, he was playing a tenor. By that time.

and I'm very certain that Bud heard Pettis. Bud had been playing a violin, you see, by request of his family, and I'm quite certain that Bud was influenced quite heavily by Pettis before he ever heard anybody else. Bud's story is that it was Coleman Hawkins.

Well, I think also somewhere there's a story that Bud was impressed by Beesey. So you've mentioned. He might have. Bud, Beesey, the sparkling ivory keys and the shiny horn and some of those things I think have come out in later years as a possible influence on Bud.
Also, Beesey had a fantastic slap tongue, and that always intrigued any saxophone player.
There have been some Columbia records, Paul Beesey's trio. Do you happen to know who the other people are? No, I've got the records.
He was awful.
Was Weedhoff of any importance? Was it a saxophone player in that period?

You know, the saxophone at that point was really a quite new instrument. I mean, it wasn't recognized by legitimate musicians at all. And I think the first impression any of us had of a saxophone came either from Weedhoff or from the Six Brown Brothers.
Oh, yes.

And it was a fascinating instrument. It was an incredible number of keys on it. And also the fact that it's a remarkably easy one to play. Not well, but you can certainly play it very easily compared to a clarinet, for instance.

Strange how many violinists, when the music picture changed, went to a Reed instrument. Do you think it had anything to do with the range being comparable? They went to clarinet frequently, or went to alto.
Yeah.
Or was it just the fact that this was a new opening?
I think so.
The horn players had already monopolized the horn business.
Also, the horn's a terribly difficult thing. Yeah. You almost have to start it before you're bright enough to realize how hard it is. I've told this to my partner. It's not going to get very well.
Too easy to become discouraged. Yeah.

When I say a saxophone is being much more easy than a clarinet, it's because both octaves are in the same key. You push an octave shift, and you're still in business. And the clarinet, you've got that difficult transition because the lower octave and the upper are in different keys. Oh, yes.
Bud fooled around with the clarinet, too. You think that came later?
Yes. Yes.
Now, Tish was also a violinist initially, wasn't he?
Yes.
And he went to clarinet. Did Bud and Tish happen to get together just by chance? Was there any? They didn't get together as violinists, fellow violinists.

No, they were in school together, though. Now, my partner can give you this accurately. My opinion is that their families selected the instrument they were going to play. I don't think Bud picked up the tenor. And I don't think, I'm quite sure Jimmy didn't get a clarinet. I mean a cornet.

Yes. I think that also a part of this story might come from Lanigan, who being a little there senior and wanting to organize a band may have influenced them what instrument to get. Was it Jimmy McPartland's father who had the music store? He had something to do, didn't he, with getting instruments for them? Was he a teacher? He may have been a teacher.
I should know that and I don't remember.
I don't. But this is something.
Remember, Richard McPartland was Jimmy's brother, the guitar player, was two years older than Jimmy.
Was he an Austin alumnus?
Yes, I think I'm quite certain. Because he was, he probably had more influence on this.
When you talk about the Austin, can you remember offhand the five or ten people who are involved here as the Austin?
I think Davey Tuff was there. Gene Cooper was at University High. Tash was at Austin. Jimmy and Rich were both at Austin. And Bud.
Well, we have of an earlier generation, Art Grunemal. He was a piano player.
Oh yes, I knew him very well.
Did they have other piano players?
I don't know why. I thought of Art as being younger.
No, he's a little older. Or a matter of a year, maybe.
Well, Dave North was the pianist for them.
That's right, Dave North, yes.

And then they originally had an alto player with him. Who I know very well. I can't think of his name. What's Bud Hunter? I think of Bud. I know Bud, but I never associated him with them at that point.
I think he was in Austin. I don't know whether before or after. Jacobson was not an Austinite, was he?

No, I don't think so. I associate Bud, for some reason or other, with Bud Jacobson, with the South Side. And he may have been the University High, too. I'm just not certain about that. Now, there were high school bands at San High School on the Near North Side. And at New Trier in Winnetka. And when I first met, but never really got to know the Austin boys, it must have been in 22 and 3. When I was playing with the first band organized around New Trier and then later San.
Who was in that band?

Nobody of any consequence. I think the only one that was known afterwards at all was Chug Champlin, who played a whole lot of different instruments. Phil Thompson, who played the banjo. Abbie Barker. Well, as a matter of fact, many of them, because Chicago is quite a Dartmouth town, went to Dartmouth and were part of the Dartmouth-Barberi Coast.
Oh, yes.
And then they would come back and often take jobs in summer in Chicago.
Now, in the work around Chicago, the summertime work drew some of these men onto the boats. Do you ever ride the boats across Lake Michigan? Boats that had five- and six-piece bands?
No. I know they did that at that point. I didn't.

Both Bix and McPartland, whom we've mentioned, worked those boats. And apparently so did Brunus on occasion. Now, this may have been their first contact with Brunus. And it would be about 23, 24 in the summers of those years.

They also played at Lake Delavan. In Wisconsin. Well, Condon and McPartland. Oh, yes. And a wonderful amateur. We always thought of him as an amateur, Fritz Nielsen, a pianist. It's probable that Fritz was the best of the Chicago pianists.
Did that be in those years? Yes. Or earliest 20s?
Early 20s. The Chicago pianists were not very good. The white pianists weren't very good.
Well, how did Joe Sullivan come up? Out of nowhere?
I can't tell you that, because I don't know. I've known him ever since, but I don't know.
There are several pianists around Chicago. And you're right. None of them were remarkable, except Joe.
Yeah.

Joe hit the first water. And the rest of them came from outside. People like Stacy, for example, was not a native. No. Chicago. I don't know how long he lived in Chicago, but he started out in Russia.
Yes. Well, I certainly don't associate art with the early days at all. No. He didn't.
Well, he showed up by 1928, but that isn't the 24 that you're talking about.

And I can't remember when I first ran into jazz. He was sort of a legend to me for quite a long time. Art Grunewald, on the other hand, I don't want to not pay proper attention to him. He really was good. Probably still is.

He's capable, and yet there isn't the strong jazz elements, which came just a few years later. Art plays a nice steady piano, and if he weren't playing with a jazz band, you might not identify it as great jazz music.
I suppose not. But he's capable enough with a jazz band.
Supply the beat, and he rides along very nicely on it.
He also liked the Lower Indiana stuff, associated with it, because he's the only person I've ever known who could play that Boneyard Shuffle.

And he made arrangements. When he was working with the Gold Cat Orchestra at WGN, he would arrange mix tunes for them. He took delight in that. He arranged the Wolverine's Limehouse, which they recorded. However, that was a different Wolverine's. It was Voino's band, but a band that apparently didn't contain any of the early men. And so he was quite understanding, at any rate, and rather sophisticated for a Dixie former. Here again we come to that question, whether without New Orleans there might have been a high order of art in the dance music around Chicago. We now think that it's quite artful, because there are many conscious efforts to draw progress and draw high virtuosity out of the men, and develop the most out of the music. In your opinion, they did not, in those years, acknowledge that New Orleans was the only influence.

No, they did not. And I've often wondered where the influence crept in without their knowing it, and I suspect, of course, it was through Paul Merez and Rapolo, and those fellows. And Brunus. One thing that used to surprise me, I originally played with a little band around a country day school. This must have been as early as 20. Five, four pieces. Not a Dixie-Line combination at all, but with a C-molly saxophone, that kind of lead. When I graduated, I think by learning how to play an E-flat, to the New Trier group, which is a little more sophisticated, they were more sure of themselves, and they were inclined to wad up it a little more. And they were playing pop tunes. This was the day of, let's say, Avalon, well, San, from World War I, Japanese San Man type. But you could still play them in tempo, all right. Pretty good tempo. Then the San Band, maybe just because it was a tougher... San High School. Yeah. The San Band was inclined to really plaster these tunes. I mean, they really hit them. So there was a decided beat to what they were doing. When we ran into the Austin Band, of course, they blew us right out of the room. I can remember when we had a battle of music that was very common those days in the Sovereign Hotel on the north side for, I think it was a San Prom or something like that, where we were at opposite ends of the auditorium. They'd take a vote at the end of a battle, and we won it, hands down, because they could dance to us, and they couldn't dance to the others, or at least they didn't know how. It was a very amicable proceeding, since the Austin boys knew that we'd given our shirts if we'd been able to play as well as they did.
Do you remember anybody in the San Band of that period?

I think Bill Tell, a banjo player, who later played with those Vocalion Wolverines records, was one. I'd have a lot of trouble putting it. Oh, Roz Metzger. We had two pianos. Roz Metzger, who went on and became quite a darn good piano. He's now president of Footcone and Bellingham. It was led by a violinist, like the Ramblers. The reason I brought that up was because I think this increasing attention to beat, as the bands that I ran through got to be a little better, to the point of the Austin band growing the same way, but with more confidence and more intention to really wallop this music and get a thing going, was pretty much independent of New Orleans. At least it was until you heard the Rhythm Kings, because the Rhythm Kings records, they rarely could, I don't think even then they could record with a bass drum.
No.

Don't impress you as being a walloping type of thing. And when you heard the Rhythm Kings, the thing that impressed you more than anything else was the rhythm that they had going without a high volume.

is the records then do omit this element of a more marked rhythm than we would suspect for the dancing fad of the period. Well, I wonder if dancing, and we find that the number of dance halls, the number of dancers, the number of dance bands, were increasing very rapidly in the early 20s, whether it wasn't the dance that had a great deal to do with drawing out the full potential of rhythmic music or jazz, and that maybe if it hadn't been for dance, there wouldn't have been jazz.

Now that you remind me, John, you know, we thought about that and we argued about it. In the first place, one phenomenon in the jazz music business is that practically no musician can dance at all. And it may be like, you never see a waiter eating, so maybe it's a chance that you normally see them playing. But the point is that very few jazz musicians like dancing. At the same time, we were conscious as early as 25 and 6 that dancing required us to play more rhythmic and better music than if we were just playing without it. In the first place, it meant that you had to play for a prescribed length of time. You couldn't change rhythm, for instance, at all. And you had to suit yourself within reason. It generally ended up that you did a more orderly job and a better one and a more rhythmic one if people were dancing to you than if they weren't.
This was a discipline, then.
Yeah, and we were conscious of it.
Did you notice in the performance of the New Orleans bands an adherence?
the requirement for dancing, the careful adherence to rhythm. Were they usually playing for dancing?

Yes, the Fry's Inn, of course. King Oliver? Yes. Oliver was generally playing for a larger group. The Fry's Inn wasn't a very big place. And I didn't get out to hear Oliver half as much as I wish I had. It was too hard to get to. It was twenty miles from my house. Twenty miles were sixty miles now.
It was over on the lake shore when you heard him at the Royal Gardens or Lincoln?
Yes. My memory's a little dim on that but I seem to remember hearing him at Midway. He also played at the Plantation.

Did you ever play at the Midway Gardens? There were colored bands and I don't remember specifically Oliver. People like Cook's band played out of White City and possibly Midway and Dinell Howard talks about playing with bands but I can't recall Oliver specifically.
By 1926 at least everybody in the Oliver band or associated with it as far as we were concerned were legendary as being wonderful musicians.

I wanted to dwell on these early years to get as much information as possible from your recall of them because they probably were impressionable years and you were eager to get what you could out of the entertainment and what you were hearing and what you could apply. Do you remember after the New Orleans rhythm came groups that had strong influence? For example, did Bruna's group at Valentino still represent a big jazz band or were there other groups in 1925 or were you away from Chicago at that time?
I was completely away then. I was back only occasional summers. Yes.

All right. Then let's go back a little earlier if we can. Do you remember that these fellows had reason to look to music as a permanent livelihood? The call for musicians was growing, wasn't it? They could work five nights. Yeah. And they could work their summers and it was fairly pleasant work. Did the decision arise because they recognized their talent or did it arise because they enjoyed the music so much? What do you suppose was behind the Chicago boys deciding to become musicians? You didn't but you must have known something about their feeling.

Yes, I did. I was in a sort of a different economic bracket in a way. That was one reason. Another was I was predestined for college and law school. And I had an extremely strong-willed father who, that was, let's say, half the reason. I think the other half was the fact that I didn't feel that I was very talented at all. In the case of the Austin boys, they didn't, as a rule, have any definite profession to go into or any particular thing that they were aiming at. I would say that because they loved it so much and they were as dedicated as you can be as a teenager to something like that, that the way for them to drift into it in the face of this increased. In the face of this increasing demand for musicians was easy. It was a line of least resistance. I don't doubt whatsoever that Jimmy McPartland's father put up an awful battle about the two of them going into it. I'm quite sure he did.
Well, yet he was a musician, wasn't he?

Yes, he was. But I don't think he wanted them to do that particularly. It was like Jimmy Dorsey's father. I mean, he didn't want them to get into it, although I think he started both of them on trumpet.
Probably in both cases, the fathers didn't realize that music might develop to the economic security that it did for a long period at any rate.

It's still, in Chicago, it didn't have the connotations it did in New Orleans about the places where you worked, the Storyville type, for instance. It was, it, but they still were, it still was a Capone town, if you remember.
Yes.

And the, the, the joints were joints and there was no other way of describing them. Some of them were fancier than others, but you were still working, uh, for what was then a pretty darn good rate of pay. I'm not sure whether Petrillo was in them, but the, but the, the, the, the white union was, was pretty effective. And in its interest in getting the weight scale up for the pit bands, which is all it was really concerned with, the large mass of fiddle players, it managed to get the scale up so much that it was very tempting. It was for me when I got out of college. The, I had a, uh, Ben Burney wanted me to play accordion with him, uh, on a five-year contract at 150 a week. Didn't, uh, this is 29.
Didn't, uh, Bill, uh, Priestley get into something of that sort, too?
Well, when Bill Priestley left Princeton, he had one year of architecture to do at Columbia. And so he played with Warrings.
While, uh, while he was going to Columbia. Oh, is that so? It was simultaneous?
Yeah, which is quite a feat, I might add. Five shows a day at the Roxy's.
Well, he didn't travel very much with the bandwagon.
Uh, he traveled one whole summer with them. Oh, yes. But then, uh, then he went to, to, um, uh, Germany to study architecture.

It, uh, seems that music was changing rapidly enough that, uh, if you couldn't change with it, it might be left behind. Frankie Quartell says that he dropped out of music. He just couldn't keep up. And, uh, you would recognize him, of course, as an earlier generation, five or ten years of Columbia. And, and he never could quite, uh, rid himself of what was back up. Frank Snyder, uh, as a drummer, too, might have grown out of date. Well, now, uh, the new fellows coming up in Chicago, uh, those who, uh, grew to prominence in the mid-twenties, didn't seem to suffer that aging quite as severely, did they? No. I mean, Jimmy's still working today, but still working today.

No, they didn't. They had a condom. No, that's a, that's a, a funny thing. There, there are, of course, there are the old legends about what happened when the, when the necessity for learning to read came up. Uh, Paul Mayers, for instance, said any time he had to read what somebody else wrote for him, he'd quit. He said that's why he started the barbecue place on North State. Um, I can remember that, I think it was George Johnson and the Wolverines, when Dick Voino announced that everybody was going to have to learn to read, and Dick was the only one who did know how. There was that absolute dead silence, and, and, uh, Johnson said, what do we do if the lights go out? They'd been playing in two or three places where they'd been shot out, and that maybe had something to do with it. I think you're right that, that the, uh, well, the, the Austin boys didn't have much to change because they were pretty young, you see, and they were on top of the world in a way. This might interest you. When I took their record east to Princeton, the 26 record that they made, uh, and played it for musicians in Princeton, they thought I was out of my head.
It was too progressive to have understood it.

They treated it as if it were a Spike Jones record, particularly when Tash would be a quarter tone off, some of those high things. They couldn't understand that at all. And, uh, but that wasn't the case when the, when the boys actually came east. They came east at a miserable time because there, there, there just wasn't much money to be made in it. But, uh, Red Nichols was smart enough to recognize that these guys had something that, that his tricky little man never would have in, at all. And so he just took them all over. Not as a unit, but always as, as members of his band.
Yeah, he used them in the recording and in the band and so forth, yes. Um, the, uh...

And they brought a whole new forest to New York. And they scared the daylights out of it. Well, Bix had paralyzed them anyway. You see, when he came east with the, uh, and I mean that, too. When he came east with the Wolverines and they played at the Cinderella roof. They didn't do any business before 11. And that was before the, that was when the musicians began to drift out of the theaters and drift out of the stage shows and wherever they're working. And then from then on to closing, they were packed. The management didn't like it because the musicians never bought, never bought anything. But, but the point was the place, you couldn't get in the place later.
I wonder if you recognize that same thing on the south side. There were, uh, early joints till 12 or 1 and there were late joints till morning. Did you happen to remember that?
I do remember that, yeah.
And, uh, I, I wonder if it wasn't, uh, for the, the, uh, same two audiences. The dancing audience and the listening audience.

Is he from New Orleans? I don't know, because I always associated him with that group.
Yeah, I don't know.

So Napoleon was, wasn't he? With, yeah, no, no. Napoleon and Sig Norelli, I think, are New York Italian boys. They're not from New Orleans. No, it's true that they certainly do play Dixieland style, but I don't think they're of New Orleans origin at all.
A lot were from Boston. Yes. Yes. And the Boston boys had imitated the Wolverines a great deal and the original Dixieland. They were their two great influences.

It was a surprise to me when I played some of the early Chicago records for Bobby Hackett in maybe 1956, and he had never heard them. He said, they knew what they wanted to do, but boy, that was pretty crude.
No, Dix himself was the influence on Bobby. Yeah, the first influence. Yeah. Yeah. Now, Gowans would have known about them. I'm quite sure. And Maxie probably. Yes.
Yes.
Because they had bands in the Mal Hallett band in Boston with Pearly Breed, had some wonderful musicians and they played all the Wolverine arrangements. Note for note.

Well, then, the Wolverine influence was very strong in the white element. Yeah. It recalls that Red Nickels wants to culvert. I wonder if that's enough in Indiana that he could have felt that influence. Hard to say. He does show more Bix maybe than anything else, and it's a leader Bix.

I think that when, well, the Indiana influence on everything in this country is kind of peculiar. It's a peculiar state. It's a, the Hoosiers stick together no matter where they go. There may be presents in New York banks and you'll find them at the Hoosier picnic at Coney Island. It's a crazy place. Full of poets, full of, of, when I said hillbilly earlier while we were talking, I didn't quite mean that, but I, I wasn't too far away from it. It's country music. Ragtime, soft shoe.

What do we think of as the folk music? Sure. Sure. Uh, now you say you've talked to Hoagie about the sources of jazz influence, and you mentioned Ragtime. And Hoagie thought that there might be other entertainment elements, and what did you say he called them?

Well, he was talking about tricky, tricky music. That meant, that's where you're, you're being clever and smart about it, and, and inventive. Uh, on the other hand, I don't think Hoagie now would say that, that jazz developed independent of the Negro. Although where-
He'd recognize the story and say, yes, there's a great deal of truth.

Yeah, and he's, he's probably right, I think his, although I can't relate it to much of his good, the best of his songwriting. Uh huh. He doesn't particularly, any more than you do in Johnny Marcer. Yeah, I think that you'd say about his songwriting that it was tricky. Yeah.

But, uh, he is often after a chord change, which is a little unusual, or, uh, melodic lines that are somewhat, uh, you hear. You, uh, are familiar with his acknowledgement that Stardust is based largely on some Bixen, on a Bix idea.

No, I didn't know that. I'm not surprised. Yeah. Uh, Washboard is, uh, is really kind of the key to almost everything he's ever written since. It's got parts in it. I can remember when the Wolverines got the record of, uh, of Washboard. Or rather, when I got the record and played it for him, and they said, my goodness, they said, Hoagie's made the record of that crazy tune.
That was the, uh, Hitches? Yeah.

With Boneyard on the other side, which is, was an impossible chorus. Uh-huh. And I tried to get Hoagie to play it about a year ago, and he couldn't. Uh-huh. It's, it changes keys about five times in one 32 bar chorus.

Uh, now, this, this, uh, changing keys brings me to a point that, uh, returns us to repertoire. Uh, I remember that the Chicagoans investigated how complex or how simple they were. And, uh, although the blues involves just a basic key and it's the simplest chord relative, uh, they tried to simplify even beyond that on occasion, didn't they?

How, how so? Gum, for example? Oh, an example of what they did in Chicago. How simple they could be? Yes, it's a two chord tune. The second, the middle chord, uh, well, it's a lot of work. It's a verse to a tune called the Eel that Friedman is generally supposed to have written. But the, uh, we've played it for hours on end. It's a B flat chord. And, uh, I think it's a, E flat 11th or something is the second chord. And that's all there is to it.
Now how can you have a tune that simple?

Uh, uh, well you can, uh, it's impossible. I can't play it on the piano, so it sounds like anything at all. And we used to try it on, on awful good pianists all the time. And Roy Barkey's the only guy that's ever been in the house that was able to play the metal, so it sounded like anything. It's a tricky sort of thing. Getting back to the, to the, to chords. You're, if you listen to Negroes singing in the south, I, I heard them not in New Orleans, but I heard them in the, uh, in the fields, or in Florida when I was a kid. Now they, it, it, it took the, in that part of the world at least, and those particular ones, it, it took the white man's training. For instance, the fifth jubilee singers, who were singing then, um, to put the, the major third into their singing. They sang in the way the Gregorian chants go, the fifth and the fourth. The, uh, back, uh, in, in the origin, uh, there's, our scale, uh, originated from, as you well know, from the harmonics. The strike a bell, and, and the first harmonic would be the octave. There was a time in, and, and not too long ago, when an octave sounded discordant to people. And the, the, it took some time before the, the major fifth, that is C to G, was acceptable. Well, once that's acceptable, then G to C is. So you get the fifth and the fourth. But it took forever to get the E in that chord. Oh. That is a major chord. The minor third came in way before that, E flat. So the minor is a much more fundamental thing, and it's why all of the old church music is that way. So your Negro singing in the, in the, in the south, as I heard them, never would sing the major third. So, what obviously happened in New Orleans was that the brass bands introduced the third. And that is, that perhaps explains where your, the rock is and shields and others. You see, we're, we're playing a little different thing than, than your Negro was playing in, in the blues, and even when he started imitating them. Then, then of course, uh, once he did, the, the, the fact that he was, uh, fundamentally of, uh, a, a, a built, it was a built-in musician, you see, and wonderful at it. Uh, the, the third came in, came in quite naturally to him.
So, so it's, it's, it's, it's the treatment of the third that, that might have, uh.
the two musics for a while, if you want to put it in its simplest terms.

Yeah, at some stage of the game, it must have been an important factor. When, before, the Negro had a chance to get hold of good instruments. That must have been quite important. When he was building his instrument, and generally beating things, when you beat something, you get harmonics, and you don't get that third. And when you sing sad music, it's always sung in the minor. And that also shows that the major third was late in getting there.

Uh-huh. Very interesting relationship there. I didn't realize it could be resolved as simply as that, and then we read through the truth. Do you remember the first band you ever heard, the first thing that might be a dance band? I'm changing our talk chronologically now to try to cover a little ground that we missed.
My guess would be that it was probably the very, very early Ted Lewis, Art Hickman, that type of orchestra.
On theater stages and clubs?

I can remember trios. I can remember the all-star trio. That was with George Hamlin Green on xylophone, and Victor Arden, I think it was, on the piano. And as the orchestras grew, it was at first thought that you couldn't have three saxophones playing at once, or the needle wouldn't stay on the record, or there'd be some money that you couldn't hear anything. Then Isham Jones was important to us because of some of the people in the band.
Well, that was later, though. That was a long 24, wasn't it? Yeah. That's about the first time you began to hear pop in.
The Oriole Terrace. Uh-huh.
The Oriole Terrace, me, let's see, well, it puts us around mid-25s, and that's when you got to the Edgewater Beach to hear that.

Yeah. They had some very good guys in the band. Nick Lucas was their guitar player, and Frankie Papilla was probably the only great clarinet, accordion player. Accordion, yeah. And Babe Nacet, who wrote Susie, we were talking about, the tenor player.
There was a generation of Chicagoans before the Austens, and you mentioned Quartell. Are you familiar with his brothers?
No, I don't remember now.
He plays trombone, and the younger brother plays clarinet.
I knew he had brothers, but I didn't.
And, um...

Tinny Scoville, Glenn Scoville, was another tenor player who was a contemporary of Don Murray's. Don Murray used to play a scene melody in a Presbyterian church in Evanston. That's how he got started. And then he changed to clarinet when he joined Go Cat. But he and Scoville both played with the Rhythm Kings.
Scoville?
Scoville. Scoville. S-C-O-V-I-W-L-E. Yes, yes.
Uh, there were a couple of people around Chicago, and I'm trying to think. Uh, they, they, uh, got in, uh, the trombonist Maxson. Remember him?
Yes. What was his name? Uh, Roy. Roy. Roy Maxson. Sure. Yeah. Wasn't he with White Man later?
Uh, yes.
Yeah.
And, uh, he's from New Orleans.
No, I didn't know that. Yeah.
And, uh...
I think I knew him. And the Benson Orchestra, if you remember, had, uh, Roy Bargy in it. And, uh, a couple saxophone players that ended up with White Man.
Of course you got to know Valle Defoe.
I, I never knew him well at all. I'd met him.
Well, he was a slightly earlier generation, I think. He was about, uh...
I saw him a few years ago.
And, um... There were a few who, uh...
Mal Stitzel.
Yes.
Is another. Who played the piano with the Rhythm Kings.
Well, I thought surely I could remember four or five of them. Uh, where does Danny Elvin... Is he, uh... Was he a little older?
Uh, he must have been, because I don't remember him as of then at all.
Got into show work.

I think, as a matter of fact, I probably first met him in New York. And then back here later. Uh, we were talking about, uh, Tony Perennis from New Orleans. Yes. Isn't he? Yes. I can't remember how early I knew him anymore.

Well, Tony, uh... In the 30s was with Ted Lewis, and earlier was with, uh, in radio work at New York. But I don't think that he came north. Until about 30. In other words, he wasn't in the firsts. Um... There was a trumpet player by the name of Lopez.
Yeah.
Remember him?
Yes. But not, not very well. Uh, Lopez... Was it Ray?
It was Ray.
Yeah.
It was of, uh, considerable influence to a slightly earlier generation than the Austin. Uh, Dooley talks about him. I guess Dooley played with him. Do you remember that Dooley had a brother in music?
No, I didn't know that. No?
Well, I've been trying to run him down. I hadn't been able to. They played out on the south side, around 35th Street, at the time that 35th Street was integrating.
Oh, yeah.
I had the first colored band, then the second colored band, then he saw these...

segments.title: Steiner introduces Squirrel Ashcraft and the interview aims
segments.summary: Steiner introduces Ashcraft as a Chicago-style bandleader and says the interview will cover New Orleans influence on Chicago and New York.

segments.title: Born 1905, a lawyer and pianist, first jazz heard on records
segments.summary: Ashcraft gives his birth year, family and law career, and says he and the Austin boys first met jazz through records such as the Friars Inn Farewell Blues.

segments.title: Bix's influence on Chicago came through records
segments.summary: Ashcraft and Steiner discuss Bix at Lake Forest and his friend Cy Welge, and whether they knew the New Orleans Rhythm Kings before hearing the record.

segments.chapter: Friars Inn, NORK and Chicago influences
segments.title: Who was in the Friars Inn band and where Wolverine sources came from
segments.summary: Ashcraft says the Wolverines did not credit New Orleans, thinks their sources were hillbilly, and lists the Friars Inn band's Chicago and Indiana/Illinois members.

segments.chapter: Friars Inn, NORK and Chicago influences
segments.title: How the two four-piece bands came together as the Rhythm Kings
segments.summary: Steiner and Ashcraft recall the Chicago meetings and Erie Cafe jobs where Brunies, Pettis and the Snyders formed the group.

segments.chapter: Friars Inn, NORK and Chicago influences
segments.title: White and Black musicians kept apart in Chicago
segments.summary: Ashcraft says white musicians seldom connected with Black bands like Oliver's, with separate unions and Black bands seen as entertainers.

segments.chapter: Friars Inn, NORK and Chicago influences
segments.title: Did Teschemacher and Freeman imitate Johnny Dodds?
segments.summary: They discuss whether Tesh drew on Dodds, Bechet or records; Ashcraft cites Kless and Goodman, and defers to Pee Wee.

segments.chapter: Tenor sax and the Austin boys
segments.title: Jack Pettis and how the tenor saxophone came to Chicago
segments.summary: Ashcraft tells how Pettis bought a C-melody sax on armistice night, ended up on tenor, and probably influenced Bud Freeman.

segments.chapter: Tenor sax and the Austin boys
segments.title: Saxophone as a new instrument; violinists turning to reeds
segments.summary: They talk about Paul Beesey, Weedhoff and the Six Brown Brothers, why saxophone was easy, and why violinists took up reeds.

segments.chapter: Tenor sax and the Austin boys
segments.title: Austin boys' instruments chosen by families
segments.summary: Steiner and Ashcraft discuss Freeman, Teschemacher and McPartland as violin and cornet starters and the McPartland family's role.

segments.chapter: Tenor sax and the Austin boys
segments.title: Who the Austin group were, and their pianists Grunewald and Dave North
segments.summary: Ashcraft lists the Austin High players, and they discuss Art Grunewald and Dave North as pianists.

segments.chapter: Tenor sax and the Austin boys
segments.title: Ashcraft's own high school bands at New Trier and Senn
segments.summary: Ashcraft describes the school bands he played in around 1922-23 and the Dartmouth musicians who worked Chicago summers.

segments.title: Summer boat and resort jobs; Lake Delavan and Fritz Nielsen
segments.summary: They mention Lake Michigan boats, Delavan, Wisconsin, and the amateur pianist Fritz Nielsen.

segments.title: Chicago pianists: Joe Sullivan, Stacy and Grunewald
segments.summary: They discuss why Chicago white pianists were weak, Joe Sullivan's emergence, Jess Stacy, and Grunewald's arranging at WGN.

segments.title: The Austin band's drive against Ashcraft's school bands
segments.summary: Ashcraft recounts a battle of bands where the Austin band outplayed his and argues the growing beat owed little to New Orleans until the Rhythm Kings.

segments.title: Did dancing shape the beat of jazz?
segments.summary: Steiner suggests dancing drew out rhythmic jazz; Ashcraft agrees playing for dancers forced discipline.

segments.title: Hearing Oliver and the Friars Inn; away from Chicago in 1925
segments.summary: Ashcraft recalls hearing Oliver at Midway and other spots, and says he was away from Chicago by 1925.

segments.title: Why the Austin boys became musicians and Ashcraft did not
segments.summary: Ashcraft explains his law-school path versus the Austin boys, their fathers, Chicago's Capone-era joints, union scale and a Ben Bernie offer.

segments.title: Bill Priestley studying at Columbia while playing in New York
segments.summary: Ashcraft tells how Priestley played with Waring five shows a day at the Roxy while studying architecture.

segments.title: Older musicians who could not keep up; learning to read
segments.summary: They discuss Quartell and Snyder aging out, Paul Mares quitting over reading, and the Wolverines' reaction to reading.

segments.title: The Austin boys' record, Red Nichols and the Chicagoans in New York
segments.summary: Ashcraft says Princeton musicians mocked the 1926 record, Nichols used the Chicagoans, and recalls the Wolverines at the Cinderella Roof.

segments.title: Early joints and late joints on the south side
segments.summary: They compare early and late audiences and moonlighting musicians like Jimmie Noone and Oliver.

segments.title: Returning to Chicago in 1928; what made the Chicago style
segments.summary: Ashcraft says a definable Chicago style existed, driven by repeated notes and rhythmic force as in Freeman and Muggsy.

segments.title: Wolverines' quiet last choruses and rocking rhythm
segments.summary: Ashcraft remembers the Wolverines at the Green Mill getting softer through the last choruses while the room rocked.

segments.title: Key changes in tunes keep rhythmic playing fresh
segments.summary: Ashcraft explains how China Boy and New Orleans tunes modulate, giving new life to each chorus.

segments.title: How much the tunes themselves mattered
segments.summary: They discuss New Orleans versus Chicago-written tunes, built-in discipline of a standard repertoire, and martial brass-band tempo.

segments.title: Tin Roof Blues, the tenor in Chicago and clarinet parts
segments.summary: Ashcraft describes Rapolo's chorus, George Johnson's influence on Eddie Miller, and how tenor changed ensemble voicing.

segments.title: Breaking down Chicago style; riffs and Bix with Whiteman
segments.summary: Ashcraft associates the style with tenor, clarinet and trumpet and one-figure riffs, and says Bix absorbed it from McPartland and the Pollack band.

segments.title: Dynamics and restraint in Chicago playing
segments.summary: They discuss use of soft playing, 'underwater', and whether restraint came from not knowing what notes to play.

segments.title: Wolverine breaks and their rhythm rule
segments.summary: Ashcraft says Wolverine breaks had to sustain and improve rhythm, and cites Bob Gillette and others.

segments.title: Indiana exchange with Chicago; Pettis goes east
segments.summary: Ashcraft notes Wolverines swapping ideas with the Rhythm Kings, Don Murray replacing Pettis, and Pettis working boats and Ben Bernie in New York.

segments.title: Harmony: Bix's whole tones and Condon's four-string guitar
segments.summary: They discuss Bix's whole-tone surprise, Condon's big majors and why four-string guitar sounds sharper.

segments.title: Improvisation and musicians' firm standards of taste
segments.summary: Ashcraft says musicians agreed ten-to-zero on what was good, with Bix never playing a note in questionable taste.

segments.title: Intonation: Teschemacher's quarter tones and Pee Wee
segments.summary: They argue that Tesh's out-of-tune effects were deliberate, comparing classical just intonation and Pee Wee Russell.

segments.title: Earl Hines and Chicago piano
segments.summary: Ashcraft calls Hines possibly the greatest pianist and describes his right hand, vibrato, tenths and Jimmy Johnson bass.

segments.title: Piano technique: octave vibrato and middle fingers
segments.summary: They puzzle over how Hines, Jess Stacy, Dave North and Bix produced octave effects.

segments.title: Piano touch, Bix and Stacy
segments.summary: Ashcraft jokes that he and Bix sounded like they used the sustaining pedal, and admires Stacy's tone.

segments.title: Joe Sullivan's 1926 record and Chicago piano
segments.summary: Ashcraft says Sullivan's 1926 record was the first driving Chicago piano, though he does not link him to Chicago.

segments.title: Arthur Schutt and the Georgians' effect on Chicagoans
segments.summary: Ashcraft says Schutt influenced them most after Hines, perhaps via the Georgians heard in New York.

segments.title: The Original Dixieland band in New York; tailgate trombone; Miff Mole and Teagarden
segments.summary: They discuss the ODJB's influence, Larry Shields' clarinet school, tailgate trombone, and Miff telling Ashcraft about Teagarden in 1928.

segments.title: Red Nichols's many recording groups
segments.summary: They discuss Nichols recording on many labels, with Miff and the Charleston Chasers, Five Pennies and Redheads.

segments.title: Jazz bands in New York in the mid-1920s
segments.summary: Ashcraft recalls the Ramblers and the dominance of records and big bands over small groups.

segments.title: Chicagoans arrive in New York; the Pollack band
segments.summary: They note the Chicagoans came 'as a breeze from the far west' around 1927 via the Pollack band.

segments.title: New Orleans men in New York: Sig Norelli and Napoleon
segments.summary: They find few New Orleans players in New York and discuss Norelli and Napoleon.

segments.title: Boston bands and the Wolverine influence
segments.summary: Ashcraft says Boston musicians imitated the Wolverines and original Dixieland; Hackett and Mal Hallett's band come up.

segments.title: Indiana's influence, Hoagy Carmichael and 'tricky' music
segments.summary: They discuss Hoosier music, Hoagy's sources, Stardust and Washboard Blues.

segments.title: A two-chord tune Chicagoans loved playing
segments.summary: Ashcraft describes a tune with only two chords and how simple Chicago repertoire could be.

segments.title: The major third and early Black singing
segments.summary: Ashcraft theorizes that Southern Black singers used minor thirds and brass bands introduced the major third in New Orleans.

segments.title: First dance bands Ashcraft heard; Isham Jones
segments.summary: Ashcraft recalls Ted Lewis, Art Hickman, the All-Star Trio, and Isham Jones at Edgewater Beach with Nick Lucas.

segments.title: Earlier Chicago generation: Quartell, Don Murray and Glenn Scoville
segments.summary: They discuss Quartell's brothers, tenor players Murray and Scoville, and how Murray began.

segments.title: Other Chicago-era musicians: Maxson, Bargy, Stitzel, Danny Alvin
segments.summary: They run through Roy Maxson, the Benson Orchestra, Defoe, Mel Stitzel and Danny Alvin, with Ashcraft knowing few well.

segments.title: Ted Lewis, Ray Lopez and south side bands
segments.summary: Steiner asks about Parenti, Ray Lopez and Dooley; Ashcraft knows them little and the tape ends mid-question about 35th Street bands.
